Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Monday, 18 November 2024 at 2.00pm
(Day 061)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Hilbert Chiu SC with Ms Joanna Davidson for NSW Health
Mr Tim Jap for NSW Treasury

THE COMMISSIONER: Good afternoon.
MR MUSTON: Good afternoon.
This afternoon, Commissioner we have a panel
comprising Louis Kastoun and Julian Cornelius of NSW
Treasury, and Alfa D'Amato from the ministry. They are
sitting in front of you in that order, your left to right.
<LOUIS KASTOUN, sworn: [2.01pm]
<JULIAN CORNELIUS, affirmed:
<ALFA D'AMATO, sworn:
THE COMMISSIONER: Mr Chiu, you are here for health?
MR CHIU: I am, with Ms Davidson, thank you.
MR MUSTON: I should probably allow the representative
from NSW Treasury to announce their appearance.
MR JAP: My name is Tim Jap, Commissioner, for NSW
Treasury.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Leave is granted for you to
appear.
MR JAP: Thank you.
<EXAMINATION BY MR MUSTON:
MR MUSTON: We'll go through each of you respectively
Mr Kastoun, could you state your full name for the
record, please.
MR KASTOUN: Louis Kastoun.
MR MUSTON: And what's your role within the NSW Treasury?
MR KASTOUN: Executive director of the health and stronger
communities division. It's part of the policy group -
budget policy and budget group within NSW Treasury.
MR MUSTON: You have co-authored with Mr Cornelius
a submission which is undated, but it was received,

I think, on 11 November, responding to issues paper 3 of
2024.
MR KASTOUN: Indeed I have.
MR MUSTON: That, Commissioner, is exhibit M1, which is
[TRY.0001.0001.0001].
THE COMMISSIONER: Thank you, I have that.
MR MUSTON: Insofar as you are aware, the contents of that
submission are, to the best of your knowledge, true and
correct?
MR KASTOUN: It is.
MR MUSTON: Mr Cornelius, could you state your full name
for the record, please?
MR CORNELIUS: Julian Cornelius.
MR MUSTON: And could you tell us what your role within
NSW Treasury is?
MR CORNELIUS: I'm the director of the health team in the
policy and budget group.
MR MUSTON: You, as mentioned earlier, were one of the
co-authors of the treasury submission received on
11 November?
MR CORNELIUS: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: And to the best of your knowledge, its
contents are true and correct?
MR CORNELIUS: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: In due course, that will be tendered as part
of the bulk tender, Commissioner.
Mr D'Amato, could you remind us of your full name?
MR D'AMATO: Sure. Alfaister Davis D'Amato, or Alfa
D'Amato, and I'm the deputy secretary, CFO, NSW Health.
MR MUSTON: You have prepared or previously participated

in a joint statement dated 27 November 2023 with
Ms Willcox?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Which, Commissioner, I think you'll find at
[MOH.9999.0005.0001].
You have also, I think, prepared a statement dated
4 April 2024?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Which, Commissioner, is [MOH.9999.0763.0001].
You have now participated in the preparation of
a joint statement with Mr Carr and Mr Onley?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: I will ask you this question about that
statement.
MR D'AMATO: Sure.
MR MUSTON: To the best of your knowledge, are the
contents of that most recent statement true and correct?
MR D'AMATO: Yes.
MR MUSTON: That statement, Commissioner, is exhibit M6,
which you will find at [MOH.0011.0091.0001].
Now, in the evidence that Mr D'Amato gave us
in November of last year, he walked us through the health
budget setting process from the ministry's perspective.
I might ask from a treasury perspective if either of
you representatives of NSW Treasury could walk us through
in a narrative way the way in which the health budget is
set from treasury's perspective, perhaps starting the day
after a budget's been delivered and working up on the point
where the next budget is delivered.
MR CORNELIUS: I'm happy to take that one. So after
a budget is set for the year ahead, we'll have - that
budget year will be established and then the forward

estimates will also have an estimate of health's budget for
the next - for the next 10 years. That will be set in our
forward estimates.
During the course of the year, we have a - the budget
process tends to take the same shape and form most years.
It can move around a little bit, depending on whether it's
an election year, and other variables might change it a
little bit, but normally we have a regular cycle. It
involves a budget submission being received around February
and March of the year before the budget.
During the course of that --
MR MUSTON: Just pausing there, the budget submission
that's received in February or March, what's the general
nature of the information that's contained in that
document?
MR CORNELIUS: So that will typically include some
analysis from health around system performance, around
risks and pressures, and around new policy measures. And
so when we receive that submission, we prepare advice for
government, and we'll typically consider what we think is
the base funding requirement for the year ahead, looking at
emerging cost pressures and other risks that might have
come up and be included in that submission.
MR MUSTON: So let me just take it back a few steps.
System performance information that is contained in the
budget submission, what sort of metrics are you looking at
there?
MR CORNELIUS: It might depend a little bit around what
parts of the system may be under pressure or may be
relevant to the budget submissions that have been received.
For example, in the submission that we've lodged, we
provide an example around planned surgeries, and certainly
for that measure, the evidence that was presented
referenced how the planned surgery performance had been
going and the impact of the pandemic on that.
MR MUSTON: Dealing with that one, the performance metric
that you had regard to or were provided with for the
purpose of considering whether or not to increase funding
for the purpose of ploughing through some further elective

surgery post COVID was, in essence, the wait list as it
existed at the time that the submission was made.
MR CORNELIUS: Yes, that's correct, so depending on the
nature of the proposal we'll have different data points.
I think most relevant are the dataset that the Bureau of
Health Information publishes on a quarterly basis that
would provide insights into emergency department
performance, planned surgeries and other parts of the
services.
MR MUSTON: Just pausing there, that information where you
referred to emergency department performance, that's
waiting times in emergency?
MR CORNELIUS: Correct.
MR MUSTON: And insofar as elective surgery is concerned,
again, waiting times for elective surgery?
MR CORNELIUS: Yes.
MR MUSTON: The sorts of things that are easily measurable
and are routinely published by the Bureau of Health
Information.
MR CORNELIUS: Correct.
MR MUSTON: Coming back to where that fits in to the
budget process, you mentioned the example you give of the
increased funding to - I think it has been described as
getting over the hump of post-COVID elective surgery. You
have also referred to the base funding. Was it
contemplated that there would be some increase to the
standard base as a result of the process you have gone
through there or was that rather a policy proposal for some
short-term funding to enable this hump of unmet elective
surgery to be dealt with?
MR CORNELIUS: Yes, that's the latter. For that
particular proposal, it was time-limited funding.
MR MUSTON: But can I come back to the base, starting with
the base. Perhaps just tell us, in words that the
non-economists amongst us will understand, what the base
comprises.

MR CORNELIUS: Effectively the base is the full recurrent
budget for health, which is, I think, around 33 billion or
so, and then the escalation factor that is applied forms
the base in forward years.
MR MUSTON: So the base comprises an operational budget on
the one hand; is that correct?
MR CORNELIUS: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: And then a separate capital budget on the
other?
MR CORNELIUS: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: How do those two sit together and how do they
work?
MR CORNELIUS: The capital budget again is budgeted on the
sum of individual projects that are approved, and there is
also a provision in health's forward estimates as well for
future works.
MR MUSTON: So let's stick with the operational component
of the budget for present purposes. How is the operational
base calculated? How has the figure been arrived at?
MR CORNELIUS: Well, I think that just reflects the
history of incremental budgeting over time.
MR MUSTON: You might not know, it might be such a piece
of ancient history, but do any of you have any
understanding of where, in history or how historically the
figure was originally arrived at?
MR CORNELIUS: I don't.
MR KASTOUN: Before my time as well.
MR MUSTON: Would it be an assumption that, at some point
in history, a decision was made by persons unknown that an
amount of money was the amount that it cost to deliver the
public health system at that point in time, and that's then
grown incrementally or organically since?
MR CORNELIUS: Yes, I think that's a fair statement.

MR MUSTON: And I don't say this critically of anyone, but
would it be right that the assumption one makes is that
that base is an adequate amount to deliver the public
health system, save any adjustments or the like that are
required, or remains an adequate amount to deliver the
public health system?
MR CORNELIUS: I think the amount of growth in any budget
year is dynamic and can change based on the circumstances.
So while you're correct to point out that the base is there
as it has been and it has evolved over time, the amount of
incremental funding that's provided in any budget can
change depending on the circumstances of the day.
MR MUSTON: Perhaps I didn't put my question as clearly as
I could have. As part of the assessment of the base year
to year, or as part of the growth, assessment of growth, is
any calculation or quantification made of the cost of
delivering the public health system, the actual cost?
MR CORNELIUS: I'm not sure I'm not following the
question.
MR D'AMATO: In terms of cost, we determine actually, on
a yearly basis, actually every six months, the unit cost of
delivering services in the activity based funding model,
and that actually is used to inform the state price. So we
are confident that then we know the cost. Obviously it's
all driven by the demand as well and what we can, within
the budget, afford to deliver. So in terms of costs, I'm
confident that we certainly know where the costs are and
how we calculate that.
MR MUSTON: I'll come back to my question. So we start
with the base figure, which has, since it was arrived at at
some point in the past, been allowed to grow through the
application of a growth factor year on year. How is that
arrived at?
MR KASTOUN: Just for clarification, as well as that
growth factor, incremental decisions by government to also
increase for other purposes.
MR MUSTON: So in terms of the decisions to increase for
other purposes, how do they fit into the equation? Are
they the NPPs that we've heard some evidence about?

MR KASTOUN: Correct, yes. So new policy proposals, as
well, as I guess, the initial starting point with an
assumed sort of baseline growth, as part of each budget
cycle, there is an assessment of the adequacy of that
funding and that takes into consideration the capacity of
the baseline funding to address growth requirements, cost
escalation issues and, in addition to that, the ministry,
the minister, would also provide proposals that relate to
new initiatives, basically, proposals to either expand
existing service delivery or, indeed, completely new
initial initiatives.
MR MUSTON: Just so we can put it into some context, do
you have examples? Could you give us some examples of the
sorts of new initiatives historically that have been the
subject of NPPs or this incremental growth?
MR KASTOUN: Yes, I think this year's budget, '24/25
included a package to enhance the operation of emergency
departments, for example.
MR CORNELIUS: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: Just in very broad terms, what did that
involve?
MR KASTOUN: In terms of?
MR MUSTON: What was the package to enhance emergency
departments? Enhance in what respect?
MR KASTOUN: So basically, to increase the capacity of the
emergency department from the perspective of urgent care,
the capacity to enhance discharge capability within the
hospital system.
MR D'AMATO: If you want I can provide some more
information. The package was worth around 421 million over
the forwards and the current and around 6 million in capex.
That includes a number of initiatives that will be rolled
out throughout the next four years, including single front
door, urgent care services, alternate care pathways,
health/ambulance metrics and managing the ED demand. There
were also some elements in regards to Hospital in the Home,
short stay units, discharge concierge, so it was
comprehensive, all dedicated to emergency departments.

MR MUSTON: With the ultimate objective being to divert
people away from the emergency department where the view
was they probably didn't need to be there, they could be
treated elsewhere?
MR D'AMATO: Yes, that's correct.
MR MUSTON: For example, in an urgent care setting?
MR D'AMATO: Yes.
MR MUSTON: And to the extent that people did arrive in
the emergency department and needed to be transitioned
through into either an acute setting or discharged quickly,
some of these proposals that you've just run through were
aimed at creating efficiencies in that process?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct. In regards to efficiencies,
access - improving access as well. Obviously the aim of
some of these initiatives is to, if you want, avoid, where
possible, patients to attend the emergency departments, so
looking at low acuity and diverting to other areas of the
system and all - like, for instance, urgent care services.
But that also means that, effectively, what we have left,
we have capacity, with more complex patients which leads us
to more cost pressure.
MR MUSTON: In relation to that particular proposal, was
any consideration given to the impact or the extent to
which a thin or failing primary care market might have been
contributing to the increase in presentations in emergency?
MR D'AMATO: It is basically one of the key areas that
we've been trying to address, in particular to urgent care
services, where at the moment, these are funded by the
state and we are not able to claim Commonwealth
contribution for some of these centres, and there was
a decision made a couple of years ago, so this funding, in
effect, is to extend the funding for this initiative for an
extra two years.
MR MUSTON: Was consideration given at that time to the
possibility of addressing the problem more at its root
cause and filling the void created by thin or failing
primary care markets?
MR D'AMATO: From my point of view, perhaps, that's

a consideration for the policy area. We certainly find
ourselves in making judgment calls in regards to the
funding, the costing of the - in particular, what is
required to support the policy area, but I can only assume
that it was the number one priority. But given that,
either because of the lack of the primary health care
sector or the lack of availability of GPs, this was the
best solution for us in order to also, as I say, achieve
other policy objectives, such as access.
MR MUSTON: Can I come back to - I think we were stepping
through and I interrupted you, but the base figure,
a growth figure and then there's the incremental increases
through NPPs. Perhaps talk us through how that growth
figure and the NPPs are dealt with throughout the budget
process coming back to our narrative walk-through the --
THE COMMISSIONER: Just before you do, this isn't
a criticism either, but you started with an exploration or
raised the issue of whether the base amount is adequate to
deliver the public health system. That begs the question
what the public health system is.
MR MUSTON: I was going to come back to that, but I can
deal with it now.
THE COMMISSIONER: You are? I will leave it with you.
MR MUSTON: I'm quite happy to deal with it now.
The Commissioner has just raised, as to the adequacy
of the base, either now or at any point in the past, to
deliver the public health system, it raises a real question
about what the public health system comprises; do you agree
with that?
MR KASTOUN: Yes.
MR MUSTON: The evidence that we've heard over the past
12 months or so has suggested that health is, in effect,
a bottomless bucket, in the sense that you could continue
to pour money into it and that, assuming some level of
inefficiency which is unavoidable, by and large, that money
would be well spent on meeting health needs of people
within the community. But a decision has to be made at
some point about exactly what the cap on that spending is
and at what point do you turn off the tap.

Are those three propositions broadly acceptable to the
three of you?
MR KASTOUN: In terms of the cap, I think it's important
to recognise a number of dynamics at play. Firstly, the
fiscal environment we're in at the moment, and I guess
drawing attention to our budget papers. I mean, the
budget's been in deficit since 2019 - since 2019/20, and
for this year, it's a budgeted deficit of 3.6 billion and,
at the moment, forecast to continue with the deficit to
'27/28, albeit reducing.
Secondly, the tension around gross debt and, you know,
at the moment gross debt is forecast to increase to around
200 million by '27/28. That has consequent implications
for interest costs for government, and so one of the sort
of fiscal priorities for government is to try and, I guess,
bring a responsible approach to spending and to try and
stabilise the state's fiscal position, from an operating
perspective and also from a debt perspective.
You also have the tension of other competing
priorities in other portfolios. So I guess, reflecting on
my portfolio responsibilities, for example, you know,
government has priorities with regard to out-of-home care,
it has priorities with regard to disability, domestic and
family violence, social housing and so on, and investment
in those areas also has a bearing in terms of the impacts
on the health system.
So there is a tension there between, I guess, the
competing priorities that exist within health, within other
portfolios, but also trying to balance it against the
fiscal bottom line.
So ultimately, from a treasury perspective, with the
advice that we have, the evidence that we receive, we put
forward the best advice that we can. You know, I will draw
to the point that it is ultimately the decision for
government in terms of the level of funding that's provided
across portfolios. So our role is to provide advice around
the fiscal parameters and to provide advice on the merits
of funding proposals that are submitted, not only from
health but across multiple portfolios and, ultimately, it
is a trade-off conversation for government through the
expenditure review committee to determine appropriate

allocations across various portfolios, having regard to its
fiscal priorities as well.
MR MUSTON: So the consequence of that is a responsible
government that deals with - well, a fiscally responsible
government has a confined amount of money that it can use
in any given year to deliver on its competing - the
competing demands that are placed upon it --
MR KASTOUN: Indeed.
MR MUSTON: -- health, education, housing, no doubt a wide
array of others. Decisions have to be made, ultimately, at
a political level, informed by treasury and each of the
various ministries about how that finite bucket of money is
to be divided up between those competing resources.
MR KASTOUN: Correct.
MR MUSTON: Insofar as health is concerned, the practical
reality is there's probably not enough money, bearing in
mind any reasonable carving up of that money between the
various priorities, there's not going to be enough money to
deliver everything that everyone wants at any given time.
That's a reality. Would that be right?
MR KASTOUN: Ultimately, it is a trade-off - it is
a trade-off conversation for government. Yes. There's
a finite amount of funding available in any given budget
cycle and, you know, it is about prioritising across
competing priorities.
MR MUSTON: Maybe I should put it a bit better. As part
of that prioritising process, there will inevitably be
things that, say, the health ministry or members of the
community might want that, as part of the balancing of
priorities, are not going to be funded through the health
budget in a given year.
MR KASTOUN: I think there's a practical reality to, you
know, what government can reasonably fund, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: There will be margins, though, won't
there? The funding will always be there, I assume, for
acute services to make sure that, for example, planned
surgery takes place within a clinically appropriate time,
so that would be a clear goal of health?

MR KASTOUN: Yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: So the money will be there for that; it
will be in other things like community health, prevention,
et cetera, where there's possibly a bigger debate about how
much money is made available for what than in the provision
of acute care services in our public hospitals; would that
be right?
MR KASTOUN: So look, from a treasury perspective, I guess
our key focus each budget cycle when we receive new policy
proposals is to, I guess, consider those proposals that are
basically the category of urgent unavoidable or address
immediate risks, and that is to ensure that core service
delivery can continue. And then that's not to say that we
don't actively consider and provide advice on the merits of
other proposals, you know, relating to, I guess, new models
of care, for example, you know, new initiatives and so on
and so forth.
MR MUSTON: Coming back to the base, though, and this
question of what is to be delivered as part of the public
health system, we've got the urgent care that someone might
need, if they have had an accident or they have some part
of their body fail, if they turn up at hospital and need to
have, say, their appendix removed - we'd gather that that's
probably largely non-negotiable in the health space. If
you walk into a hospital and you need to have something
done urgently, you will either have it done there or be
transferred to a hospital where it can be done and receive
that lifesaving treatment.
MR KASTOUN: You'd certainly hope so, yes.
MR MUSTON: That's those core urgent or acute aspects of
it, but then as to what sits around that in terms of those
non-urgent acute forms of care, as part of treasury's
function, does it have visibility of what's on the table
and what's off the table at any given year as part of the
public health system, and in determining whether or not the
base is adequate?
MR KASTOUN: Yes, would you like to answer that,
Mr Cornelius?
MR CORNELIUS: I think it's fair to say we don't have the

same level of visibility around community care as we do for
what's in scope for activity based funding. So, you know,
I think the system could benefit from a bit more structure
and clarity around the scope of services that are provided
in the community, because we don't have as much visibility
on that as we do for other parts of the system.
MR D'AMATO: Look, I think that certainly, you know, the
data that we provide treasury is not at the kind of level
the same way we manage the system, but I do think that in
regards to the base we also need to acknowledge that we're
still stepping out of COVID and perhaps it's a bit
difficult to identify what is the right base in this
environment where there is relatively still a bit of
volatility.
But during COVID, it's fair to say that the budget,
you know, we had to flex in regards to the envelope, the
growth, because we had to respond to anything. Now, we
are - as we're stepping out, we are trying to identify what
is the base, the proper base. I also reflect before COVID,
we experienced a relatively stable environment
economically, fiscally, and we were able to optimise
efficiencies, and the way we funded the hospitals through
ABF was working well, back then, in a stable environment.
Now, I don't think we have a stable environment yet, and
that's probably the difficulty, in my opinion, to set the
base.
MR MUSTON: It's probably more a matter for tomorrow and
Thursday, but at a ministry level, what level of visibility
does ministry have of the particular array of services that
are being offered as part of the public health system in
each of the LHDs?
MR D'AMATO: Look, we obviously collect all the data, so
we have visibility across the sector in respect to whether
there are in-scope services or out of scope services, so
I would say that we have visibility across all system.
MR MUSTON: When you say "in scope or out of scope", are
you referring to within the ABF?
MR D'AMATO: I was referring more in terms of what the
Commonwealth would contribute towards, or not. Apologies,
there. It's just some of my terminology.

MR MUSTON: That's okay. So "in scope" are services for
which the Commonwealth is making a contribution of some
sort either through ABF or via another grant or funding
stream?
MR D'AMATO: Yes.
MR MUSTON: "Out of scope" are services, when you refer to
them, which are being funded wholly by the state?
MR D'AMATO: That's correct.
MR MUSTON: So you have oversight or some visibility of in
scope and out of scope services. Even amongst those
services, though, do you have a sense of what the patchwork
of services that are being delivered to a community
actually looks like?
MR D'AMATO: Yes, yes.
MR MUSTON: In what way?
MR D'AMATO: Either through the activity that we deliver
or some of the, if you want, even NGO grants that we pay to
community organisations to deliver services on our behalf.
And also I think it's important to note that when we choose
to engage with some of these third parties, we do it
because there's a benefit overall to the system in that
ultimately, in many cases, they provide services that
either would be too costly for us to be investing in and
deliver, or they provide the community type of services
that actually allow us to discharge patients earlier than
otherwise.
MR MUSTON: In terms of the activity, what does the data
that you have available to you about activity within the
LHDs actually tell you about what's happening on the ground
in the LHDs?
MR D'AMATO: Okay, well, the activity section is not under
my division, however, it's fair to say that, through a
costing exercise that we conduct every six months, we
actually trace every single patient in that we actual
calculate the cost of every single encounter from the
moment that they arrive to our emergency department,
throughout the emergency department, when they move into
acute settings, when they actually discharge, and wherever

there is special level data that we can link, we can trace
the cost and we can actually trace the patients for the
purpose of planning and the purpose of clinical, if you
like, information.
MR MUSTON: Just one last question about the base funding.
In terms of discussions and treasury's consideration of the
adequacy of the base funding and the extent to which it
requires adjustment, is there a discussion that happens
between the treasury and the ministry along the lines of,
"Here are the services that we think we can provide within
the budgetary envelope we've got and provide well; here are
services which we think the community needs, but we're not
currently able to provide them and they are lower
priorities to those that we are providing within the
budgetary envelope. If you want us to provide those
additional services you have to - you'll have to increase
our funding?" Is that a discussion that happens as part of
the budget process?
MR CORNELIUS: Yes.
MR MUSTON: How does that discussion work into the
assessment of the adequacy of the base?
MR CORNELIUS: So the budget submission is prepared by the
minister and so there is a prioritisation process before
that submission comes to treasury. So there may be
discussions internally around some of those service issues
you've mentioned. There'll be a prioritisation process
internally and then the submission will come to us and
we'll provide advice to government around our assessment of
those proposals.
MR MUSTON: And so again, these are the NPPs that we're
talking about or is this part of an assessment of the
adequacy of the base itself?
MR CORNELIUS: The two things happen in parallel,
effectively, yes.
MR MUSTON: Maybe just explain how that happens in
parallel and how it works.
MR CORNELIUS: Typically when we have the budget
submission, we will need to provide some advice around what
is essentially critical to maintain current service

outcomes, in the first instance. So there might be some
technical adjustments, accounting adjustments, other cost
variations, and things like that that we feel will need to
be funded in order to maintain current service outcomes.
So typically our advice will prioritise those things
first; and then we'll turn our mind to the new policy
measures or service enhancements, and we'll provide advice
around what we think the policy merit of those initiatives
are based on the evidence that has been provided and our
conversations with the ministry; and then there will be
some consideration around, you know, how those proposals
link in with government's sort of broader priorities and
fiscal capacity as well.
MR MUSTON: I'm just trying to understand at what level
this assessment of the adequacy of the base to meet what
has been provided is undertaken once it reaches treasury,
accepting that, by the time it gets to you, it's no doubt
had its origins in an LHD where decisions have been made
about what is needed and what can be afforded, that then
passes its way up through you ministry and then ultimately
to you.
MR CORNELIUS: In terms of the consideration of the
adequacy of the base, the performance metrics that we spoke
about earlier are pretty integral to that conversation.
For instance, we spoke a little bit about the planned
